extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, research managers, and stakeholders in scholarly publishing
extracted.subtask_short: combating reviewer burnout in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and criteria for reducing reviewer fatigue and improving the peer-review process in scholarly publishing, including incentive structures, reviewer recruitment, workflow changes, and use of AI. Focus is on making review more meaningful, efficient, and equitable while preserving human judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address root cause of burnout (lack of meaning and fulfillment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burnout... stems from a lack of motivation. Burnout is not only physical but also psychological and cognitive. It often arises from engaging in activities that feel devoid of meaning... Ultimately, burnout is about a lack of meaning and fulfillment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce cognitive friction and create space for experiential fulfillment so reviewers can explore meaning, significance, and new discoveries in their work rather than performing meaningless tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce cognitive friction by removing tedious, repetitive tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove the tedious, repetitive, cognitively meaningless tasks from peer review; what’s truly taxing is the cognitive friction caused by meaninglessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools (notably AI) to automate or streamline repetitive administrative or screening tasks so reviewers can focus on intellectually rewarding aspects; aim to cut review time to a few hours where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand and diversify the reviewer pool (equitable distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding the reviewer pool to include more contributors from non-Western countries, such as India and China, can help. Currently, most active reviewers are from Western countries, leaving a large untapped capacity in other regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively recruit and include under-represented geographic regions to distribute workload more equitably and tap additional capacity; consider training and incentives targeted at new reviewer populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make peer review more rewarding — prioritise recognition over money
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary incentives are secondary; recognition is more important. The fundamental need of human beings is recognition — the desire to feel important and appreciated. Currently, all the glory goes to the authors... But what do reviewers get?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide meaningful recognition (e.g., linking reviewers' names to reviews, career-relevant credit, prestigious invitations). Invitations to review should evoke the same sense of importance as invitations to write an editorial or opinion piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market peer review to increase prestige and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing peer review better could also make it more attractive. Targeted campaigns could engage researchers and make peer review an aspirational goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run high-visibility campaigns (analogous to iconic ad campaigns) and expand global initiatives like Peer Review Week to build pride and aspiration around reviewing and counter the perception that reviewers are exploited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reviewer recruitment by improving effort-to-reward ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is increasingly perceived as a distraction... If researchers don’t see value in reviewing (i.e., the effort-to-reward ratio), they may view it as a distraction and avoid it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrably make reviewing beneficial for reviewers' careers and status; communicate concrete rewards and benefits to increase acceptance rates for review invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reviewer completion rates and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting reviewers to start and complete reviews on time is a key challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide stronger incentives, reduce time required to review (via AI and streamlined workflows), set and promote ambitious turnaround goals (e.g., days/hours rather than months), and remove administrative blockers that delay completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI for manuscript screening and reviewer matching
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can improve the matching of manuscripts with reviewers, ensuring reviewers receive papers that align with their expertise and interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy AI to improve reviewer-paper fit to increase engagement and speed; careful matching can make reviews more intellectually rewarding and reduce declines and delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI to assist reviewers with drafting and structuring reviews (but preserve human judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can help structure and edit their notes into coherent reports... AI-generated comments can sometimes resemble those of human experts, but missing human attention could be detrimental. Reviewers must still critically engage with papers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow AI to help non-native and native speakers with articulation, organization, and clarity of reports while requiring reviewers to validate, critique, and add human insight (skepticism, nuance, empathy). Avoid over-reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer secure, publisher-provided customised AI tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of letting reviewers use AI independently, publishers should offer secure, customised tools specifically designed for peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide vetted, secure AI platforms tailored to editorial workflows to protect confidentiality, ensure appropriate use, and standardise assistance rather than uncontrolled third-party use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label AI-generated assessments distinctly from human peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated reports should not be labelled 'peer review' but could instead be termed 'AI-based technical assessments' or 'developmental reports.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain transparency about the source and role of AI outputs to protect trust and set correct expectations for authors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement reviewer training and reviewer ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Several solutions emerge, including reviewer training, reviewer ratings, and AI tools to assist with writing reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide formal training to raise review quality and deploy rating systems to recognise good reviewers and incentivise improvement and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve focus on novelty, quality, integrity and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers must still focus on novelty and quality, helping improve the paper... ensuring research integrity and reproducibility is vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AI for technical checks and assistance but keep human reviewers responsible for evaluating novelty, interpretive insight, quality assessment, and integrity-related judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment and evaluate acceptance of AI-based peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether authors will accept AI as peer reviewers is another question — one we would need to explore through low-risk experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run controlled pilots to test author and community acceptance of AI assessments versus human peer review; use results to guide policy and deployment rather than assuming acceptance.
